narrative:
Shopify engagement (2026-05-21) scanned one of H1's most mature programs ($90K–$200K critical bounty, 1188 public GitHub repos). Three passes were run: bucket-hunter Pass A (80 candidates, 14 s3scanner-flagged, 14 AccessDenied on recheck), secret-hunter Passes A/B/C (0 verified candidates), and takeover-hunter (1369 raw subdomains → 100 strict-cap → 60 CNAME → 1 subzy VULNERABLE → 0 confirmed after two independent disqualification gates). Zero reports were drafted or submitted.

The takeover pass surfaced a significant structural observation: 54 of the 60 CNAME-bearing subdomains in the alphabetical-cap-100 sample all resolve to wc.shopify.com, Shopify's internal wildcard redirect cluster (live A record 23.227.38.33). This is Shopify's own infrastructure; none of these subdomains are individually dangling. Adding wc.shopify.com to cname_hub_skip with an exact match would have reduced the effective CNAME candidate pool from 60 to 6 before subzy, eliminating 90% of subzy scan cost on future Shopify runs. The Cargo Collective FP that was ultimately disqualified by two existing rules (subzy_body_recheck_required + subzy_known_fp_patterns) came from the remaining 6 non-hub CNAMEs — both defense layers fired correctly.

The Cargo Collective fingerprint engine has now produced false positives in three consecutive engagements across three completely different hosting platforms: bc-seek (SendGrid edge), int-watsons (AWS ELB), and shopify (Shopify PaaS *.shopifycloud.com). The common thread is that Cargo's fingerprint pattern fires on any generic nginx/Apache 404, regardless of the CNAME endpoint's actual service identity. The existing subzy_known_fp_patterns entries are per-endpoint-pattern rules (*.sendgrid.net, *.elb.amazonaws.com), but this engagement makes clear the rule should be expressed as a wildcard: Cargo Collective fingerprint fires on bare 404s universally, not just on specific CDN endpoints. A generalized rule requiring actual Cargo branding in the live body would subsume all three per-endpoint rules and eliminate future one-off additions.

Pass B (codesearch) in secrets correctly identified the vendor_repo_credentials anti-pattern: three Vietnamese Shopify-app developer bootcamp repos (trantuananh-17/product-reviews, XuanTho2k/Simple-Sales-Pop, trunghoang12202/avada-training-app) all carry the identical Avada marketplace npm registry token. This is the fourth time the vendor_repo_credentials pattern has fired; the previous rules captured template repo-name patterns. A direct repo_name_skip rule on the 'avada' glob would catch this specific recurring cluster before cloning. The Avada token itself could also be suppressed via detector_ignore, though this is lower-priority since the vendor_repo_credentials heuristic already identifies the FP class at the repo level.

Pass A (trufflehog org scan) exited after scanning only 56 of 1188 repos (~4.7% coverage) in approximately 63 seconds — far below the 2700-second floor set by passA_timeout_floor_secs-d3ea2. This is not a rules-layer issue: the timeout floor rule tells the wrapper to allocate ≥2700s, but trufflehog itself appears to have an independent early-exit condition (possibly hitting GitHub API rate limits on the org enumeration call, or trufflehog's own internal scan limit). The 1132 unscanned repos include Shopify/shopify-app, Shopify/cli, Shopify/ruby-lsp, Shopify/sorbet, and other critical infrastructure. If revisiting this engagement, Pass A should be re-run with explicit per-repo targeting (Pass B style) focused on the high-value repos that trufflehog missed, rather than the blind org scan. Additionally, the strict-mode cap (alphabetical truncation to 100 subdomains) silently dropped all shopifycloud.com and shopify.io subdomains whose names sort alphabetically after the shopify.com entries in the list. A round-robin truncation across seed domains would give more uniform coverage.
